blocks.x: How long did you have the Harman's?

Well, let me see, two, three years or something. Is that so? Yeah. You followed Cook? Followed Cook, yeah. That's right. Cook went to White City, that's right. I see. And then after King came out, I don't know what happened to the planet King, what he did or anything, but…
He went to Europe, you know.

That's right, he went to Europe, that's right. He went to Europe and the next year, Paschal, who used to play with Henderson. Paschal came in, Paschal got the band, he hired me as banjoist and ranger. Oh, I had made some arrangements for King's band, and incidentally, this might seem humorous, one of the boys came up to me and said, have you heard Red Nichols and Biff Moe play Ida, Sweeties Appleside? I said, yeah, I got the record. He said, why don't you steal that arrangement, arranging for the band. I said, what? Don't insult me. Steal it, arrange that off the record? I said, I wouldn't do anything like that. What are you talking about? I got mad. About two weeks later, I made the arrangement. Brought it to rehearsal and that boy, just like they played it and we played it, just like that. All the kids said, oh we know where that's from, that's from Red Nichols, Biff Moe's record. And so that started me to, when you couldn't get the arrangement, they'd say, Charlie, get that and get your record, let's play that. And then, and then, and then, Singing the Blues. Singing the Blues, I did the same thing, Singing the Blues, yeah, arrange that. And I laugh about that many times because, I'll tell you when Duke first came out with those five saxophones, I think, and we was playing at that, oh it's a copy club, man. And they used to play on the radio, you remember, what was it, six o'clock or something, they had a broadcast? I was glued to the radio. I was waiting for them to open up. And so, when he added, I was telling Mikey, when he added those extra saxophones, I began to hear some chords, I said, what is that chord? He's using, what is that? And, I said, what is that? It was by tonality, but I didn't know it then. See, one chord was in one key, and the other rest of the chord was in another key. So, I said, now I know what I'm going to do. I said, I'm going to go and buy those records, bring them home. I bought the records, bought seven dollars, had a whole load of the records, they had seven and a half, bought them all Duke's records, bought them home, and put the, I had a portable, phonograph with a photograph, right up by the piano, and I sat down at the piano and played with the thing. And I found out that he was taking the G7 chord, raising the fifth, lowering the fifth, putting a minor ninth in there, which gives three tones of the D flat chord, D flat, F, A, A flat, which is a D flat major chord, and that would fit right in, that's a lowered fifth of a G7, and a raised fifth of a G7, and a minor ninth in there. And that, now, later on I found this by tonality, but I said, well, that's what you call a triple altered chord. In the harmony books, we had to call it altered chords. When you raised a lowered one tone of the original chord, you call it an altered chord. So I knew enough of music, you know, and I said, oh, and I started making some arrangements. So I went around on the north side and peddled some of the arrangements, you know. And I had quite a kick out of it. Who just had your arrangements? Oh, yeah, Elmer Kaiser. Did you? I arranged for him about seven years. He had a very progressive band for a time, yes.
A very progressive band, yes. A young Chicago kid.

Well, it was, yes, it was a regular dance hall band. It wasn't a jazz band, it was a dance hall band. But when I bought these arrangements up there, they got a big kick out. Then I made some of my own. By studying Duke style and some of the other guys, I began to develop a little bit myself. And I progressed from that straight. And I started to be known as an arrangement.
What were some of the things it is for Clever King? Do you recall that?

Oh, well, I made, I made, I think I made the first arrangement of Rapson in blue around here. First dance arrangement of Rapson in blue. I remember that because we got lots and lots of compliments. And Elmer Kaiser came in and played against us one night and he wanted to know who made the arrangements, so I did. And so I turned around and copied off the score and sold him an arrangement. And then I arranged for him for about seven years. I did some arranging for Giron's Paradise for the business agent, now the union, for Carlin. Yes. And Dan Russo used to have the band at the Age of Water Beach in the Chinese Chopsui place. I made arrangements for him. Then later on, Charlie Strait. That was a band. Yeah, Charlie Strait was a wonderful pianist too. That was earlier really, wasn't it?
Or was it, 25? I was still in the 20s there.
Still in the 20s. I made arrangements for Charlie Strait.
He was active later, but I think his good band was in mid 20s. Yeah, in mid 20s.

And then I wrote, then I had three little girls and I said, well, maybe I said try to write something, make some money. So, well, in the 20, I think 1920 and 21 I wrote that 35th Street. And I had written Skizics. You know the little Skizics in front of the paper? Yes. Or the cuter song Skizic. I remember it too. And I took it downtown and they kept it for about a year. I forget the publisher. They kept it for about a year and did nothing with it. And then I wrote another, I wrote another little Foxtrot and I carried it to a publisher. I forgot to copyright it and I was such a hurry to get down with it. I was so inspired with it. And they lost it, they said, and I never heard nothing more about that. So from then on, as soon as I wrote something, I got it copyrighted there. And so, in this writing, I had three wonderful little girls and they were wonderful children. They weren't bad at all, they were wonderful kids and they inspired me. So, I want to tell you, I'm going to jump ahead of myself to tell you about Fraternity Records. They recorded my Moonlight Mexico, which was a Spanish 3-4, totally different from anything I'd ever written. And Dick Noel of NBC's Breakfast Club, he recorded, this was about two years ago, and they recorded in Hollywood with Norman Luboff's Choir Byers. A beautiful record. I'm sorry I have, I think maybe I might have it on the tape there. And the rock and roll was in, and nobody bought the song.
Well, sometimes, yeah, sometimes those things are slow starters. Yes. I mean, they're always for a period.
Well, it just, it came out just about when everybody, the rock and roll, the kids.
The rest of it was raised in the sand.

Yeah, the rest of it was raised in the sand. And it was just too pretty and it just wasn't the timing. It was the wrong time for it to come out. And the, I had worked with Lou Douglas for a while. Lou Douglas liked a lot of them. I had about, written about 20 songs by then. So, he came to my house one day and I, he went over the first five and said, I like all these five. Let me have them see what I can do. So, Tommy Leonetti came to town and he submitted one to Leonetti. And so Lou and Leonetti thought it was from Out of This World. And they said it was too close to the other old song, Out of This World. That is, the lyrics were. The music was totally different and they were crazy about the music. So, they got a lyric writer to write another lyric to it and he wrote, When You're In Love. We recorded the song in Universal Studios with Lee Gillette A&R and the record sound beautiful. Everybody was enthused. And somehow in my heart, I was sad. I didn't know what was the matter. I was sad. I had copied the score for Douglas. Douglas, Lou Douglas made the Rangers. So, I copied the score. I got such a good handwriting, a lot of the Rangers want me to copy for them. So, I was copying for Douglas and so he said, Charlie, you got a hit. But somehow or another, I felt depressed. I felt like it wasn't going to happen. Here's what it was. Johnny Mercer had written a song of the same title, totally different music, for the picture Seven Brides for Seven Brothers or something like that. Yeah. And they had it in that picture. So, when mine was at this part, at least the lyric writers had written the same title, same idea. They had never heard Johnny Mercer. Johnny Mercer had never heard this. And so, the record never was released. In the meanwhile, RCA Victor recorded with Frankie Lester singing. And here, Danny Bellock's band had recorded two. So, I had three records on the song and didn't make a dime and it wasn't released because of the similarity of titles. Because the other, there's an agreement between the publishers, if one comes out with the title first and the other one didn't know about it, and he comes out with the same title, he will automatically withdraw and leave the first one. So, I had, so, yeah, I got three recordings on the song and didn't make a, and that's what it was, that premonition.
It's too bad you couldn't have simply changed the title and used the same one.

Well, I told Archie, Archie Levinson has, he's the publisher, and I told him one day, I said, why don't we put my original lyric back on there? So, he said, well, he says, I don't know, we got it printed up and everything and they might release it someday. I said, I don't think they'll release it because it's similar to the titles. I'm still, I'm gonna still see them because the tune is a beautiful tune. I got it on the tape here, I want you to hear it.

Well, this, this boy that I used to work with, this Italian boy, he wrote a song and he asked me to, in fact, you took it down. Uh-huh. And, uh, it was real fine. And, uh, I was playing some records over one day at my house and I ran into Perry Coleman and he sang the same number, just a different title, different record. It was so close together you couldn't tell. Yeah. We never had heard it.
A coincidence. A coincidence. Just a thousand of miles away and direct coincidence like that.

I took it back and took the record over and he heard it and he said, well, can you imagine this? Oh. A song that come to him. Mm-hmm. So, who else was writing in the, in the period you started? Do you remember any of the fellas around town? Uh.
You started as an arranger, didn't you? No, I started, I started playing violin. I was with this man playing violin. Well, I mean with your writing though, you started with the banjo. Uh-huh.

And, uh, the banjo became so prominent, prominent that I got a banjo. And, uh, then I went to the Regal Theater in 1929 and we had a wonderful band there. We had Red Top playing trumpet and he was later with Cab Callaway, he was playing a tremendous trumpet.
He was with Dave Payton?

Dave Payton, yeah. And we played all the toughest shows and played band numbers too. Every week we had to play a band number. And they featured me several times on the banjo. I played the world's waiting for sunrise, you know, Melvin' Chords and whipped it up. And several other numbers. Hebe-jeebies I think was another one we used to play there.
Wasn't Bud Scott also there? Did you play by?

Bud Scott gave me the job. Oh. Bud Scott, his wife went to California and she liked it so well that, uh, she told him, come on out here, I'm not coming back. So Bud met me on the speech and said, Charlie, I want you to have that job. And, uh, and he said, I told Dave Payton, he said that you can come up and cut everything they got on the paper and then a little more too. I said, oh, I think I can do that. I said, alright.
You have to do that to work with Dave. Yeah.

Oh yeah. Yes, yeah. Yes. Yes. And, uh, so Bud Scott told me, he said, you come around and see Dave, come on. He says, I got to go to California. My wife won't come back to me, say, come out there, she's crazy about California.
Was that before or after Fess Williams?
No, Fess Williams was, uh, no, Fess Williams was there. Then Fess Williams left and Harold Bacquet came and he was a master of ceremonies.
But you were there a while during Fess?
I was there, 29 and 30, yeah, 1929 and 30.

Did you happen to record with Fess Williams? I was there, they made, uh, one record in the name of Fess and his Joy Boys or something. But that might have been earlier. No, I think that was some of the, that was a little earlier.

I think that's when he first came from Louisville. Oh yeah. I made arrangements, the first arrangements I made to be recorded were made for Red, uh, what's Red's name? You know his brother played trombone? Red, huh?
Oh gosh, I can't think of his name.

Isn't that awful. What did Red play? Trumpet. You see we had Fats Robin that played the straight trumpet. Red Temple was. No, and Red played the second trumpet in the shows and on the band numbers and on the dance numbers where they, we had, we had to play for dancing couples or dancing singles. Why, Red played the first trumpet and he took off, jazzed it up and I mean he really, he really played. I know who you're talking about. Yeah, I know you do.
Where was he from?
What did he from?
I don't know where he was. He played Evansville, Indiana wasn't he? Someplace in Indiana. Someplace in Indiana. He's better played trombone.

Uh, Reeves. Reeves, Reeves, sure. Reuben Reeves. Reuben Reeves, that's it, Reuben Reeves. Well I made the first arrangements for them to record. They recorded for Brunswick Records I think. Some old arrangement. they started using the augmented chord, copying a little bit of Frenchmaster Debussy, you know Debussy. And so that was the first time I used the consecutive augmented chords that, you know, you heard so much about it and you figured you'd better do a little Debussy, use a little augmented chords in there. And they liked the rings very good. Of course, in the background I just put the sax on and hit the leg, da da da da. And then Ruben got took off on a trumpet. Was this a part of Peyton's band?
Yes, part of Peyton's band, but Ruben got them. Did you record with them?
No, I didn't record. They only had about, they had a small band. They didn't have a full band.
That's right. Those became fairly famous records.
Jasper Taylor was the drummer. And Ruben went with Cab Calloway after that.
Yeah, the collectors are very much interested in that because Ruben did so well. One of them he imitated Louie. Yeah, yes. And they call him River Reeves because he did it so well.

Did you know Feather and Gill was here? Yes. Yes. I gave Feather and Gill 30 records, old records, Joe Olive and all the old records. And he was supposed to give them back to me. He was gonna record and do something and give them back to me and I've lost track of the man. He's in New York.
Somebody said he was in San Diego. Well, he's traveling around a little and he's in artwork now.
It's not working. I gotta try to contact him and tell him about that even though it's awful late.
Yeah, but those are collector items. You can't get them records now.
No, I know they're the collector's items. Well, I didn't realize it at the time. Well, you've got a tape machine, have you? I've got a tape machine.

Well, Ike knows. I know most of the fellows around have them. So, ultimately, we'll get them together for you. You just keep in mind what it is you're after and we'll get them for you. I'll take both of them. Oh, you can dig up stuff, man. You don't know about it. There's one of Ike's that I haven't been able to get yet, but we'll get it one of these days.
Ike, didn't I find your four reasons and bring it to you? Yeah.
Yeah, on the first cut. Frankie Jackson. No, no. That's the late cut you got. Oh, is that so? Yeah, that's the last cut I made. Oh, yes.

Well, whatever it is, I put it on my tape and then I brought you the record again. I brought it on tape. Yeah, I brought it on tape. Because I wonder if there was something you did on the banjo there on the grab. Yeah, that was made by… And on the other side, it was two, three records. Bill Johnson, bass.
Yeah, bass, yeah. Called Ake Robertson's Bull Fiddle Band. Yeah. And Count Turner on the banjo. Yeah, yeah. And I was playing banjo and Bobby Warren fiddle.
Yeah, yeah.
There were quite a few of you fiddlers around in the early years. Now you went to banjo, what happened to the rest of them? They tried to make it to the middle of the fiddle.

Wyatt Houston was one of them that was a classical fiddler that turned to jazz and he really could play it. He played all the Joe Van Nudie stuff. Is that so? And all the Eddie Saw's stuff. I tell you what we did, we had a job. The booking agent asked me, he says, can you get a little string band together? There's no piano in the roadhouse. We're out at 111th Street. I said, yes, I'll get you. So I got Milton Hinton. You know he's big in New York now. I got Milton Hinton. He was in school, still in school. He'd been trying to play a little fiddle. And I said, you never play a little fiddle with that bass fiddle. I said, ruin your hands, you can't do it. You just can't do it. And at that time I bought a tenor guitar, a real good tenor guitar, Viga. And it was a beautiful thing. I ripped the devil out of it, see. I got him Hinton on bass, myself on the little guitar, and Wyatt Houston on violin. We went out this roadhouse and stampeded the place. The man…
I remember when I go like when you had the trill.

The man went out, down the street, there was a roadhouse, two, three roadhouses close there, like a corner or something. Went down there and bought the other band from the other place to hear us. Wyatt played a tremendous jazz fiddle and double stops galore. I never heard about his playing jazz. I don't think… Never recorded it. Never recorded it, no. But he really could, he really… See, he was a graduate of the American Conservatory in violin.
He knew so much. In the wintertime.

And he had tremendous. And then he was a student of it, too. And he had a fast ear and he picked up stuff that the trumpets would play and he'd slide his fingers on the strings, you know, and to the plane he'd slide it and he'd twist the strings, shove the strings in like you do on the banjo, see. Make a quarter tone, see. Yeah. And we did pretty good until, I don't know, I think the prohibition agents or something happened and they came in and we had to get another job. We went down and made an audition at NBC. And, oh, I'll tell you who came through Chicago. And, what's this lyric writer that wrote with, Andy, was it Andy Rezaff? Andy Rezaff? Andy Rezaff? Andy Rezaff. Andy Rezaff. Andy Rezaff. Yeah, he came through Chicago and he had a, he wanted to do a little thing on the radio, a little skit about musicians and a little numerous thing, a little bit on the art of Amos and Andy, but musicians came on. So he heard about our trio. So he came out the house and we did a rehearsal and he did some funny jive talk and we played. So it sounds so good. We went down to NBC and made an audition down there. And they, they owned up to it. It was awfully good. He came and congratulated us and said, gee, gee, and Wyatt really played some fiddle through double stops and harmonics and then all in swing, swing fiddle. You know, Joe Vanuja style, 80s style style. And so they said, well, we can't make up our minds. So Andy Rezaff, Andy Rezaff had a big name. You know, a lyric writer. We thought Joe was going to get on NBC. I did finally get on there with Sammy Williams' Aunt Jemima program in 1937. I was bandwagonist and guitarist on that program. The Pell player. Yes. He's tremendous. Fantastic memory and fantastic ear. I tell Nike, he brought a fellow up for me to take a song down. The fellow was singing in the cracks. And so Sammy said, he's singing near a D flat to be a singing C. That's a year, huh? Oh. So this thing with NBC, they liked it, but they couldn't make up their mind. You see, they had Amos Nandy and they didn't want anything to interfere with it. You see, that's what it was. See, what we should have did was take it over to CBS. So we made the audition. Audition was all right and everything. So that didn't pan out. So we jobbed on the north side with the little trio, my wife, Houston, myself, and Milt Hinton. And then I think Prohibition agents rated some places or something. And everything got tight. So Milt Hinton got a job with cab. He went with cab too. That's when he went with cab. And then I think I jobbed around and jobbed around. Finally this Angemiima thing came up. Sammy Williams got the Angemiima program. We were on then 37 and 38. That part of 37, first about six months, six, thirty-eight.
Would you give up fiddle in this period that you've mentioned? Yes.

I had some kids from school. I lived around the corner from DuSable High School. And I had some kids that Professor Dyett sent me. He knew that I would teach them very good fundamentals. And I had some violin students. I had some bander students too. In fact, I taught Jimmy Noon's nephew. Henry. Henry Ford. No, Henry Ford was a bass player. Jimmy Noon's nephew, his last name was Henry. He was from New Orleans too. And Jimmy Noon sent me because he knew that I would teach him right, you know, and take patience with him. And he developed a very fine band choice. And he switched over to guitar later on. A pair of good guitars too, they tell me.
Well, I remember, it was Jimmy introducing somebody, his nephew, and I thought maybe Henry Ford was in the same group. Yeah, Henry Ford's a bass player. Yeah. I guess not.
Henry Ford was one of the original bass players with King Cole.
Did you do any recording? No.

I made, yes, I hate to tell about it. No, we had, during the time that we had this little string band, I wrote a tune and carried it down to Mayo Williams who was with Decca. And Mayo said, who is that, whipping that guitar? I said, that's me playing guitar. I said, but that's a tenor guitar. I said, I can't play a Spanish guitar. So he says, well, he says, you ought to get a guitar. I said, you know, make them better and bigger now. So I says, he said, but anyhow, I want you to make a record. He said, George White, he said, George White's up for a recording. He said, so I made the, but I'm telling you, I didn't tell anybody I made the records because I was ashamed of the tunes that they picked. The tunes were rotten. Sad old blues and there wasn't nothing to them. And I think that after they, after they were recorded, I think that, I don't think they released them. I didn't have enough interest in them to even find if they released them because I was surprised that whoever picked them. Well, you may remember them.
I've gotten a lot of early Georgia and one of these days you'll go over them. Yeah. But this was in the mid to early 30s. Yes.
Mm-hmm.
When did you record in Georgia White? Thank you. I recorded with Georgia Blackwood.

I don't know what that was. It seemed to me it was on a, I believe it was an OK record. Yeah, he was A&R director for OK. I think it was an OK record. Yes. Georgia White. Yeah. Georgia White. Georgia White. Georgia, she was singing and Richard was playing the piano and we had a bass fill. I think Lindsey was on bass and I was playing. I think you went with Sammy Stewart or something. You went away and I think that's when I recorded with them.
Yeah, I remember recording with Georgia. Yeah.

Richard Jones. Richard Jones, we call him Miney Jones. He died of a heart attack, you remember? Yeah. Yeah. Oh, I knew him. Yeah. Oh, I knew him. Oh, I knew him. Yeah. Oh, I knew him. Yeah. Oh, I knew him. Yeah. Oh, I knew him. Yeah. Oh, I knew him. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. and they had a bass fill. I think Lindsey was on bass and I was playing.

Yeah, I made records with him. I think you went with Sammy Stewart or something. You went away and I think that's when I recorded with him because... Yeah, I remember recording with George. Yeah. Richard Jones, we call him Miney Jones. He died of a heart attack. You remember?
Yeah.

And you know, let me tell you, excuse me, I could, I don't know if it was the day before or the week before he called me up. He said, Charlie, get your tunes together. We're all set. He said, get everything you've got and write some more. He said, we're all set. I'm going to be the A&R director for the new Mercury Records. Excuse me. He says,
right around the corner from me.

Yeah, yeah, sure. And he said, we're on the South Street. He says, we're little, but we're going to go. And I just felt so enthused. I was so happy. And then about a week later, he had an heart attack and died. So, it kind of upset me because we have a, we've got a boogie-woogie called Canal Street Boogie, Richard Jones and I wrote. And, you know, I thought, I said, well, I was feeling good. And then I, when I heard about him dying, I felt so very bad. He was such a, he always liked me. He knew that I knew so much more music than he did. See, he didn't know very much music. Did you know him in New Orleans? Slightly. But when he first came up here, then, he saw me playing violin with Whitley's band. And he told me who he was. He was from New Orleans. He had, what did he have, a cripple leg, I think? Yeah, he's stiff-legged. He got shot from the knee. Oh, yeah. And, and, he always liked me.
He was always trying to do something.
Always, yeah, yeah. He wanted to put me in,
he told me, I'll put you in that, ASCAP. Yeah. Yeah. I'd be in there with you. Yeah. And you don't have to worry. He says, I'll get you in there for $15. And I ain't done enough to join.
Yeah. Well, that's what he wanted to do with, we had this Canal Street Boogie and I had some other tunes.
All the Canal Streets are, the New Orleans Canal Street, aren't they? Yeah. We have the Canal Street in Chicago. Yeah. Yeah. It's Canal Street in New Orleans.

So, when I was writing this other, this other thing, I thought about him many times. I said, didn't you write, he really tried to get me ahead and he called me up. I told my wife and family, I said, Mr. Jones called me up and told me, he said, don't worry, you're in.
It all depends on you. That was the first record I would make. Yeah. With Richard. With Richard. I sang.
Yeah. That was OK. OK, that's right. He was a man for OK.
How'd you happen to come up to Chicago? Was there a job waiting for you?
No, I came up to go to the Chicago Musical College.
Oh, yes.

I was studying the violin and I was interested in the piano and also in the harmony. And then when I heard some of those guys doing all this stuff, you know, as far as my classical training, I wanted to find out
what they were doing.
So I wanted to study harmony and find out, which I did. It was the most wonderful thing I ever did was study harmony in Chicago Musical College. and I really did. I had to pay.
I want you to hear this lyric.

This is In the Good Old Days in New Orleans. In the good old days in New Orleans, arsher loaves and fried shrimps were a dive. Rice cooked just right with ham and red beans with a quart a top of claret wine. In the good old days in New Orleans, nickel shows were where we took our queens. Dixieland jazz music in the cabaret that was living in the good old days. Now down here in this little minor part, here's Bolden, Morton, Bunk, Bechet, Nunez, Ori and Joe, Joe Oliver, Bacquet, Freddie, Freddie Kepp as we know, Leon, that's Leon Rapolo, Nick LaRocca, Jack, Dodds, Picou, Teot. They gave us New Orleans jazz, took us from the razzmatazz. Thanks, New Orleans, for those good old days. In those good old days in New Orleans, quat you did them in a pail of wine. Just one Picayune bought you some greens, and ten cents a pound coffee was fine. In the good old days in New Orleans, we bought nickel sodas for our queens. Dixieland jazz music and all the cabarets, that was living in the good old days. Now see, I couldn't get, I don't know, Glazer and Louis could have took this material. The publishing rights alone would have meant thousands of dollars. I would give them the publishing rights if they let Louis cut this thing, see? Oh, take your time.
They may come to you.
So, I want you to hear that first little, first little, little, I want I could hear the
two. You sit down for a minute and I'll tell you what we're going to do.
Bye-bye.

Bye-bye. This is January 3rd, 1961 and the subject of our interview is Mr. Charles Levy from New Orleans and you heard him read from his composition in the good old days in New Orleans. He didn't know that he was reading at the microphone but he was reading it to show me the spirit of some of the things he's written. voice besides mine and Mr. Levy's will be that of Ike Robinson who accompanied Mr. Levy today. The purpose of our tape or the purpose of the recording Mr. Levy is to provide the Tulane University with interviews, dictated sort and informal, relating to the New Orleans story. The Ford Foundation has provided Tulane with enough money that they can pay for the tape and we perform the interviews and they accumulate material for the history. I'd like to refer to them and learn something about your story. Would you like to take it for a little while? I kind of like to bring you into chronological stories. Sure, sure. When we were born and we were 1898 of all means. November 14th. And what part of you are? Oh, let's see. I think I was

born about a block from Esplanade Avenue, I think it was, on Barrick Street. Have you been back there lately? I haven't been there since 1914, but I said I want to go back. Oh, is that so? That's in my mind. I've seen the Monty Gras on TV and I'm telling you my heart almost cried. I'm telling you tears came to my eyes. I want to go back. Did you play when you were in LA? I was playing violin in a little group down there and just learning to put a little jazz in the violin, unbeknownst to my music teacher. Putting a
few extra notes in. Oh, we have a guy down there named Ernest Carrillo. And that guy was

way ahead each time. All right. I can hear you say something about the hearing and noise. It's a new microphone and it's possible if my contacts are bad, I'll go in there and see how they are. We may have to start over. But, go ahead with the story.

Well, you know, I was studying violin and the teacher didn't want us to play anything but the classical music, but I'd follow like all the other kids. I'd follow the bands down the street and once in a while sneak in the district, you know, with my long pants on and listen to them. I stood on the corner and listened to Joe Oliver and the bands, you know, in the district.

Everybody thinks Cliff King is the greatest in the world. He said, I can learn how to play that clarinet. And he played a few notes. He said, see I'm doing it. See the finger. And see, you got to pull all your fingers down. That's when I first had my first music talk with Darnell. But he was always my idol because he played such terrific things. And it looked like he played it so easy. And the rest of us kids, we were studying. We just couldn't do it. And Darnell had so much talent. That's what it was. He had so much talent. An inborn ear for broken cords or the notes that would pass over the cords.
We came over. Before you joined Wycliffe, did you meet any fellas? Or get to know the jazz men around? Were you in any of the joints?

Oh, yes. I went to all the joints. And I was listening because I was very anxious to better, you know, better my playing. And the boys from the post office had a little band. And of course, in those days, I always had a violin. And so they asked me to come to rehearsal. To find out if I could play good enough. And I made the rehearsal. And they said it was fine. I played good and strong. You could hear me. And besides, I played in tune. I played pretty good. So I was enthused over it. So we rehearsed quite a long while. And then every time the post office clerks or somebody that they knew would give a dance, I started playing dances. And at the same time, whenever I got a chance, I always went down. Well, all during the summer, I went down to Navy Pier where Charles Elwood was playing so I could hear Darnell. And then...
What kind of crowds would they draw? A dance crowd?
A dance crowd, yes. It was a dance crowd. Well, of course, there was a lot of people that was escaping the heat from the city. They'd go and listen to. There was a lot of listeners.
Well, they'd go to that ballroom because that's a big place.
Yeah, it was a big place. I don't know. They had a... I think they had a kind of a shell or some kind of acoustical thing there.
Well, it's still there.
If I... Is it?
Yeah. If you'd like to go out there one of these times, I'll show you that ballroom.
Oh!
It was a stage on the west side of it, and they played out toward the left. That's right. That's right. You've got to...
That's the way it is now. Mm-hmm.

And they've now converted that into the gymnasium of the University of Illinois. Oh. Uh-huh. But the ballroom, I'm sure, is about the same as it was before because all the structural beams are there. Mm-hmm.
Mm-hmm.
That probably is just as you remember.
Mm-hmm.
That's where we had Jabba this summer.
Mm-hmm. And... You know, did I tell you I worked with Jabba at the Wisconsin Roof? Yes. I thought Jabba was a real fine trumpeter.
How long were you at the Wisconsin Roof?
Oh, I think probably part of the... Well, at that time, I think they were only running a few nights a week.
That's in Milwaukee.

Milwaukee, yes. Uh-huh. Wisconsin Roof, they called it, didn't they? About the years, got a theater. Yeah. And Jabba, I thought Jabba, I don't know why he didn't get further than he did. In fact, he had a lot of talent and...
He got to be a drinker.

Is that... Yeah, he got drank too much because he wrote a couple numbers and I raised them for him. And we were at the house and... And I didn't know he had that much talent. And he played them on the horn and I think I missed a note or something. And he... And he handled his voice. And he told me this was a note I had missed. And I didn't know the guy had the most talents because I didn't think he could read too fast, you know. But he was surprisingly much better than I thought he was. And then after I went and worked with him on Wisconsin Roof, why, I had a great admiration for him.
You mentioned Cass. Do you recall now any of the other fellows there?
No, I can't recall.
Was he still around Milwaukee?
Yes, I think he was. Yes, he was around there.
Had Leonard Gay come into Milwaukee yet? No. He later came later. And you said that Bernie Young was not playing the group. No. He was around Milwaukee at that time.
I think he was. I'm pretty sure he was.
Abernathy?
Abernathy, the trombone player? Yeah. I think he was with us with Jabo, if I'm not mistaken.
I thought he might have been.
Yes, you know, he came later on with Wycliffe's band.
Now, they tell me Wycliffe played Milwaukee in about 1917. That was Darnell's first job, didn't they?
Yes, and Darnell had to put long pants on to play the job.
And they called it Wycliffe's Jazz Band, and the city wouldn't allow him to put up that song.

Word jazz, and he called it the Ginger Band. Your information is perfect because, excuse me, I know Wycliffe. Wycliffe was kind of fond of me because he had seen me come up with the violin. We had roomed at the same place, you know, and he heard me practicing, and he'd say, You're going to make it. He says, You'll make it. And so a year later, I was in his band. And he told me a lot of things. A lot of things encouraged me, and told me that Clarence Lee was a wonderful violinist, but when he got a little too much money, it was hard to handle or something like that. Or he tried to play too many women or something. And Wycliffe was very nice to me.
There's another violinist around about that time, Jimmy Bell.
Jimmy Bell played a very good violin, very strong too. He played the Grand Theater, you know, in the pit there. And then he had a band of his own. I made some arrangements for Jimmy Bell's band too.
Indiana Theater.
No, it was the Grand. Jimmy Bell played the Grand.
I thought he had his own band.

Oh, later on he might have had it, yes. But I know when I first heard him. No, Jabbo, that was later. Yeah. Incidentally, do you know that Jabbo was in that little Cull of the Kids orphan band that came from the South? Yes, Jenkins. Yes. And I saw them, this is odd, I saw them on the street in Chicago when I first came here. They were a little bunch of kids. And there was one little guy there. He seemed to be in charge of everybody. He was a take charge guy. And he played the terrific trumpet. So years later, when I met Jabbo, and I went to rehearsal with his band, and I bought some of my arrangements. He wanted to use some of my arrangements, and later on he'd buy them. The more I looked at Jabbo, the more I began thinking. I said, listen. I said, did you ever play with a little kid's orphan band? And he almost jumped to the ceiling. He said, yes. I said, I remember him. I said, you were the trumpet player? And I said, I thought you were great. And he just slay on it and give him a big kick, see? And this is years later. It's funny how those things will come to you. Because I kept looking at him and thinking. And it, I don't know, this came to my mind. And now when I asked him, Jabbo had a lot of talent. And he had, he was a little bit peculiar. He, I don't know.

Well, being an orphan. Yeah. Being on his own all the time. Yeah. It was bound to affect his psychology. He wasn't as mellow as a lot of people. I don't think he is today. In fact, he doesn't even trust himself.
Yeah. Uh-huh.

He comes down here, say, midnight or something like that, after he's through with a job in Milwaukee. And he won't go to bed for two days. Oh. There's a lot of things he wants to do around Chicago. Oh. We have a recording session. He's all played out. Played out, yes. Knocked out. Yeah, knocked out. And yet he'll keep on going another night. Yeah.
Can you imagine that?
He loves to come down to Chicago. Uh-huh. He works at, a fellow his age just can't do it anymore.
Uh-huh. That's right. His age, yes.
He's over 15. They tell me that Wickliffe was a very progressive sort of fellow. Now, as a drummer, was he just smart enough to get the right men?

Smart enough to get the right men, yeah. He always had a good band. And he was a good talker and getting jobs. And when he got a good job, he could always come around and say, I got a good job. He's paying so much money a week. And I want a good trumpet player and something like that. He would get the men. Because I know one time we played a theater, the Windsor Theater on Clark Street near the vision, I imagine it was. It was the first time they ever had a jazz band in that theater. And the man said, you run the people out. And Wickliffe talked to him and used such persuasion language as the man hired us and paid us, I think, an enormous sum. I think the units gave us around $25 a week and we got $45. The side man got $45, which was a big sum in the 1920 or 21, whatever it was. And we played when the comedy came on. Then we played.
In the pit?
We were in the box. Oh. In the box. They put us in the box. And if I'm not mistaken, I think Bob Schauffner was playing trumpet then. I think he came up from St. Louis.
Did you play every show? Or just even?

Well, we played every evening. We played every show and we played only on the comedies. I think they had a couple of comedies we played about a half hour. And then we were off to pictures about an hour. We were off an hour. It was a piece of a job.
Schauffner speaks about being with Wickliffe and mentioned a place called Terrace. Now, that's why. When you said Terrace. Oh.

There was another one. The Morrison Terrace. I wasn't with him. That was before I joined him. He had played the Morrison Terrace in the Morrison Hotel. Oh. The Morrison Terrace. And that was the first time a colored jazz band, or in fact any colored band, had been in the loop, I think, to my knowledge.
Well, no.
That was before 1920. Algar had been in the loop?
In 1918, yeah. With a band that was playing when dancing became very popular. Yes. They had bands in every hotel.
Yes.
Oh, yes. Might have been with the, well, earlier he was in the loop with the Byron Brothers. At a restaurant.
Yes, Byron Brothers, yeah. At a restaurant.
And right after that, he went into a hotel.
Yes.
Maybe the Blackstone or something.
Stratford, I imagine it was. Maybe the Stratford.
I think so. You're right. Stratford. And they were there for months. Mm-hmm. Eight months, ten months. So that was one of the earliest.
Mm-hmm. Yes, I'd forgotten that. You're right.
Then, of course, several others got into the loop. Wade.
Yes, Jimmy Wade, yes. He played the loop.
And I think Sammy Stewart for a while.
Yes. Mm-hmm.
And then, of course, it became a frequent. But you may have played one of the earliest cabaret jobs. Or Wycliffe, I mean, may have played one of the very earliest.
Yes, I think he was the first cabaret job. His was the first cabaret job.
It's strange that Wycliffe wasn't recorded.

I don't know why. Because we had a very good band. He always insisted. One good thing about him. He always insisted in getting good man. And he made the owners. They'd come up with, when they wanted to come up with that three or four or five pieces. He'd tell them, no, my band is eight, ten, whatever it was. And that's the way it sounds. And that's what's going to do your business. And he was a good talker in getting jobs. Because we went up to Blue Mountain. The Blue Chipper on the Blue Mountain Road, Milwaukee. We went up there. And we had two first violins. That was Clarence Lee and myself. We had a very good trumpeter. And we had Joe Walker, Lil' Joe Walker, playing Sykes. And Harry Gray, the president of our union, was up there. He was playing with us then. And I think he was playing tuba, if I'm not mistaken. Yes. Because I think he had got the bass fiddle later on. And Charlie Hillman was playing piano with us. He'd come up from Memphis. And...
Now, Jabba wasn't with you, was he?
No. He didn't play the Blue Mountain Road. Yes, but that was much later. Mm-hmm.
Was that near Sam Picks?

Wasn't too far from Sam Picks. Sam Picks. Yes. This is a great piano player. I forget his name was playing as Sam Picks, wasn't he? No. Lil' Walker's best colored piano player, they said. I forget his name.
Not Slap Rags.
No.
Now, I remember Weaver Brothers.
Yes.
In that period.
But there was one piano player they played. He was called Lil' Walker's best piano player. I can't remember his name either.
You were the only New Orleans man, then, in Whitliff's band, or what you've been telling me.
Well, you know, after one of the other boys left, we got Tommy Ladnere.
Oh, yes.
And then for a while, and I don't know where Tommy went, if he went back to New Orleans, or he went with the Creole band. And then we had Red Allen for a while.
Did these boys give a New Orleans sound to Whitliff's band?
No, but they pepped it up because they played a hot trumpet. Well, we called it a hot trumpet then. We didn't call it a jazz trumpet. We called it a hot trumpet.
Whitliff had maybe a pre-Ellington appreciation of broad harmonies.

Yes, he probably did. He had a good ear, too, see, and that's, because some drummers don't have a very good ear. I mean, they have a sense of rhythm, but for harmony and, well, maybe I shouldn't say that because I believe it was a bad drummers. One bad drummer made us lose an audition. We auditioned for a job, and the drummer didn't have any conception at the time. And after we played a couple of numbers real good, the man we were auditioning for asked us to play another certain number. And we all called it and said, everybody got it? Yes. And we let out, and he played it. His conception of it was bad. He played it too fast, and they ruined the band. The guys couldn't play it. It was too fast. It was way too fast, and we sounded bad, and finally somebody got lost, and I was awfully ashamed. It wasn't the band's fault. It was the drummer's fault. So the man said, you better go back and rehearse a little more, boys. The first two numbers is all right, but you better go back and rehearse some more. And we felt awful bad about it. Coming back on L, I was very disgusted.
Did Wycliffe use Dixieland numbers? They were very popular then.

Oh, well, we had Tiger Reg, and you know, with Fidgety Feet, and, well, four or five other numbers that were published for the first time. But, you know, the original Dixieland. Panama became a... Panama, oh yes, Panama. We played that, yeah, Panama.
It wasn't really from Dixie sources, I think, a higher up there.
Yeah, it was, it was, it had a slightly Spanish pattern. Yeah. A slight...
And you had the blues, all the famous New Orleans type of...

Yeah, we had, we played, well, see, the man that we were going to feature in the blues, he picked these keys. He said, all right, the blues and B flat. Now, maybe that, that, we wouldn't live, Klan, most of that. Well, all right, that was his blues. All right, trumpet player, he, maybe he played his blues and concert E flat. And we'd play that, and he'd take it for his own. He'd take the circle of course, and then finally some of them, I'd play blues on the violin, and somebody would answer it. And, in other words, the trumpet, if he called the keys blues and E flat, well, that meant that he, that was his, and he was going to take most of it. And then we played the tunes of the day, like Tartle in Chicago, you know. We played those things. And then we had several rags, like Temptation rags, and just a little bit of Scott Joplin in it. It was still, some people still liked to dance to it, because it had that, well, it was rhythmic.
I suppose that was often a piano feature.

Yes, a piano, when we got kind of tired playing, we stopped him at the piano and played a couple of choruses, and he liked it. And incidentally, did you hear about Everett Robbins? He played with us at the, at the Entenus Cafe. No. He died of consumption. Oh. Everett Robbins. He made one or two rags.
Oh, yes, of course, of course. I have a picture of him. Unfortunately, he isn't here, but he joined Rice up in Milwaukee.
Yes. For a time. After we left the Entenus Cafe, he went with another band, and then he caroused so much and didn't get any rest, and he drank so much that he contracted TB.
How was, he was a, he was a, very good.
Very good and very talented.
Compared with Cass and Ovee.

Yes. Mm-hmm. He didn't have quite the, the improvising technique of Cass. Cass was tremendous. He was really tremendous. And that Teddy Weatherford that you heard, I can speak about, he was, he was among the tops too. It was, but I mean, in those days, it's not like you look back over it, you know. You look back and you remember how it was. In those days, we knew it was good, and we didn't, we just said, well, he's going to like to work with him.
Well, Teddy recorded some piano solos in India.
He did.
And they're marvelous.
Can you imagine that?
Amazingly fine.
Mm-hmm. In the 30s. Mm-hmm.
Now, you hear Teddy a little bit on one or two records that was made by the theater band.
Oh, yeah. Tate's Theater Band. Uh-huh.
Just a little bit.
Yes.
I think Louie was in the same band.
Yes, Louie came in.
He made these recordings.
Uh-huh.
The Wickliffe band, when you joined them, was where?
At the Entertainers Cafe.
Entertainers.
Mm-hmm.
Now, did you leave Entertainers when they closed it down for Prohibition, or for Padlocked or something like that?
I think, I think so. Oh, I think that's the time I told you we went to Louisville.
Oh, you went to Louisville.
You got a book in Louisville for a month.
Yeah.

And we were in Louisville for a month or five weeks. And we came back here. And then we, I think, I don't know if it's the exact time that Joe Oliver left and went to California. He left the old dream on that 35th Street. It was a colored dream on that 35th Street. And we went in there. And we stayed there. No, that was after we came from Milwaukee. From Milwaukee, we went to the, the, the dreamland. And then, I think, Joe Oliver and them, they came back to the Royal Gardens on 31st Street. And I think they either went into Waterville or they went back to the coast. Then we went, the Wickers band went into the Royal Gardens. And that's the trumpet player. I was trying to tell you, we had an awful good trumpet player in there. He might have been Kepard. He might have been Kepard, yeah. I'm trying to think. I can't remember. He went back to New Orleans. Incidentally, he was, my mother, one of my relatives' cousins, Manuel. Manuel is in Spanish. Did he ever come north again? I don't know. I don't think so.
Theo went back. He didn't want to be anything in the north.
The weather. The boys never liked the weather. The weather's bad.
They speak of Perez as if he was mainly a good first man.
I think so, yes. Yes, that's right. Uh-huh.
Uh, hey.
Mm-hm.

segments.title: Arranging off records: Red Nichols copy and Ellington's altered chords
segments.summary: After Paschal takes over King's band, Levy is hired as banjoist and arranger. He copies a Red Nichols record arrangement, then works out Ellington's altered chords from records.

segments.title: Selling arrangements to Elmer Kaiser, Dan Russo and Charlie Strait
segments.summary: Levy sells arrangements to Elmer Kaiser's dance band for about seven years, and writes for Dan Russo and Charlie Strait.

segments.title: Early songs and Moonlight Mexico
segments.summary: Levy tells of writing 35th Street and other songs, losing an uncopyrighted foxtrot, and his Moonlight Mexico record released as rock and roll arrived.

segments.title: When You're In Love: three recordings undone by a title clash
segments.summary: His song, written with Lou Douglas, is recorded three times but never released because Johnny Mercer had a song with the same title.

segments.title: Ike on near-identical songs by coincidence
segments.summary: Ike Robinson recalls a friend's song that turned up on a record almost note for note, and Levy calls it coincidence.

segments.title: Regal Theater band under Dave Payton, 1929-30
segments.summary: Levy turns from violin to banjo and joins the Regal Theater band, getting the job from Bud Scott. They play shows and band numbers, with Fess Williams then Harold Bacquet fronting.

segments.title: First recorded arrangements, for Reuben Reeves
segments.summary: Levy made the first arrangements to be recorded for Reuben Reeves, using consecutive augmented chords. Peyton's small band recorded for Brunswick, and Reeves later went with Cab Calloway.

segments.title: Lent records and Ike Robinson's own record dates
segments.summary: Levy lent old records to a collector and has lost track of him. They compare Ike's recordings with the Bull Fiddle Band.

segments.title: Fiddlers turned banjoists: Wyatt Houston and the roadhouse string trio
segments.summary: Fiddlers moved to banjo; Levy forms a roadhouse trio with Wyatt Houston, Milt Hinton and himself, and they stampede the place.

segments.title: NBC audition for the trio and the 1937-38 Aunt Jemima program
segments.summary: The trio auditions at NBC without success, Hinton goes with Cab Calloway, and Levy later gets onto the Aunt Jemima program.

segments.title: Teaching fiddle and banjo students
segments.summary: Levy teaches students sent by Professor Dyett and Jimmy Noone, including Noone's nephew Henry, and they compare bassists named Henry Ford.

segments.title: Recording for Mayo Williams of Decca
segments.summary: Levy made records for Mayo Williams on tenor guitar and was ashamed of the tunes chosen.

segments.title: Recording with Georgia White
segments.summary: He recalls accompanying Georgia White with Richard Jones and a bass player on an OK session.

segments.title: Richard Jones, Canal Street Boogie and the Mercury job that never came
segments.summary: Levy remembers Richard Jones, who tried to help him join ASCAP and was about to become A&R man for Mercury when he died.

segments.title: Why he came to Chicago: studying harmony at the Chicago Musical College
segments.summary: Levy came to study violin and harmony and wanted to know what the jazz players were doing.

segments.title: Reading the lyric 'In the Good Old Days in New Orleans'
segments.summary: Levy reads a lyric he wrote naming New Orleans musicians and hopes Louis Armstrong might record it.

segments.title: Recording opening: purpose of the Tulane interviews and Levy's birth
segments.summary: The interviewer states the date and project and introduces Levy and Ike Robinson. Levy was born 14 November 1898 near Esplanade Avenue, New Orleans.

segments.title: Sneaking into the district: Joe Oliver and Grunwald's Cave
segments.summary: As a violin student Levy follows bands and sneaks into the district to hear Joe Oliver and a jazz band at Grunwald's Cave.

segments.title: The original Dixieland band and Tony Sbarbaro
segments.summary: They work out who was in the original Dixieland band, and Levy says he knew its drummer.

segments.title: Willie Jones and early jazz fiddle in New Orleans
segments.summary: A boyhood friend, Willie Jones, played jazz fiddle and showed the others the extra notes. Jimmy Palao is mentioned.

segments.title: Joining Wickliffe's band in 1920 and learning to arrange
segments.summary: Levy plays violin in Wickliffe's jazz band at the Entertainers Cafe, teaches himself arranging from a library book, and recalls the trumpeters in the band.

segments.title: Writing 35th Street at Joe Garman's Paradise
segments.summary: After the Entertainers Cafe the band moves to Garman's Paradise. Levy writes 35th Street, which Mayo Williams places for recording, and discusses its form.

segments.title: Louisville trip, Dreamland Cafe and George Mitchell
segments.summary: Wickliffe's band plays a month in Louisville and returns to Dreamland, with George Mitchell on trumpet. They chat about Mitchell today.

segments.title: Ike Robinson's banjo lessons and joining Jelly Roll Morton's band
segments.summary: Ike Robinson coaches Levy on banjo. Morton then calls him for a banjo job and he plays with the band in Chicago, about 1927.

segments.title: Dance dates with Morton and Wickliffe's Milwaukee engagement
segments.summary: Levy played dance dates with Morton but no theaters. He also recalls Blue Mound Road in Milwaukee with Wickliffe.

segments.title: Walking bass: Bro and Johnny Lindsay
segments.summary: He recalls a bassist who walked the bass at the Entertainers Cafe, and Johnny Lindsay's four-beat New Orleans bass.

segments.title: Royal Gardens after Oliver; Cliff King and Freddie Keppard at Harmon's Dreamland
segments.summary: Wickliffe's band follows Joe Oliver into Royal Gardens around 1926. The next year Levy is with Cliff King at Harmon's Dreamland with Keppard, and King is a showman clarinetist.

segments.title: Keppard against Oliver: style and rival cliques
segments.summary: They weigh Keppard against Oliver, noting Keppard's power and that Dreamland was a ballroom while Oliver played cabarets.

segments.title: Size and personnel of the Harmon's Dreamland band
segments.summary: Levy lists the Dreamland band: three saxes, two trumpets, two trombones, and a rhythm section with Dick Curry on drums. The tape ends in garbled fragments.

segments.title: Studying music on his own
segments.summary: Levy says he studied hard on his own and played professionally only after school.

segments.title: Family land and a lawyer's theft in New Orleans
segments.summary: Levy describes his Choctaw grandmother's land and his father's property sold to a railroad. After his father's death a lawyer pocketed the money, and his mother went home to sort it out.

segments.title: Starting violin at eight and a trip west
segments.summary: A full-size violin put him off at first. His mother took him to California and then Chicago for her health, and the early Creole band in California is mentioned.

segments.title: Lessons with Charles Elgar in Chicago and return to New Orleans jazz
segments.summary: In Chicago in 1911 he studies violin with Elgar, goes back to New Orleans at about 14 and sneaks into the district with Willie Jones. Later he studies harmony at the musical college.

segments.title: Elgar's band and Darnell's jazz violin at Navy Pier
segments.summary: Levy goes nightly to Navy Pier to hear Darnell's strong jazz violin with Elgar's band and attends a jazz concert featuring Cliff King and Darnell.

segments.title: Post office band and Navy Pier dance crowds
segments.summary: Before joining Wickliffe he plays dances with the post office band and attends Navy Pier concerts, whose crowds include people escaping the summer heat.

segments.title: The Navy Pier ballroom today
segments.summary: The interviewer says the ballroom is now a university gym and offers to show Levy, and mentions Jabbo played there this summer.

segments.title: Working with Jabbo Smith at the Wisconsin Roof
segments.summary: Levy worked with Jabbo Smith at the Wisconsin Roof in Milwaukee and admired his talent, though Jabbo drank.

segments.title: Who was in Milwaukee: Cass, Bernie Young, Abernathy
segments.summary: The interviewer asks about Milwaukee musicians. Levy cannot recall some and places Abernathy with Jabbo and later with Wickliffe.

segments.title: Wickliffe in Milwaukee and his kindness to Levy
segments.summary: Wickliffe played Milwaukee around 1917 as a Ginger Band because the city banned the word jazz. He encouraged Levy as a young violinist.

segments.title: Jimmy Bell, violinist at the Grand Theater
segments.summary: Levy recalls Jimmy Bell as a strong violinist at the Grand Theater and says he arranged for Bell's band.

segments.title: Jabbo Smith and the orphan band
segments.summary: Levy recognises Jabbo as the trumpeter he saw in the Jenkins orphan band. They talk about Jabbo's personality and restlessness.

segments.title: Wickliffe as bandleader and the Windsor Theater job
segments.summary: Wickliffe was a good talker who got good men and good pay, including a Windsor Theater job paying $45 a week.

segments.title: The Morrison Terrace and early Black bands in the Loop
segments.summary: They discuss Wickliffe at the Morrison Terrace, claimed as the first Black jazz band in the Loop, and earlier Loop bands such as Elgar's.

segments.title: Blue Mound Road, Milwaukee, and its pianists
segments.summary: Wickliffe's band, with two violins, plays Blue Mound Road in Milwaukee. They try to name a local pianist.

segments.title: New Orleans trumpeters in Wickliffe's band
segments.summary: Levy was the only New Orleanian at first, but Tommy Ladnier and Red Allen later played with them and pepped up the band.

segments.title: Wickliffe's ear and the drummer who lost an audition
segments.summary: Wickliffe had a good ear for harmony. A drummer who took a tune too fast cost the band an audition.

segments.title: Wickliffe's repertoire: Dixieland numbers, blues and rags
segments.summary: The band played Tiger Rag, Panama, blues in the trumpeter's key, popular tunes and rags with piano features.

segments.title: Everett Robbins, pianist who died of tuberculosis
segments.summary: Levy remembers Everett Robbins, who played at the Entertainers Cafe and died of tuberculosis.

segments.title: Teddy Weatherford and Tate's Theater Band
segments.summary: Levy rates Teddy Weatherford among the tops and they discuss his India recordings and Tate's band.

segments.title: Entertainers Cafe, Louisville and Royal Gardens; Manuel Perez
segments.summary: They recap leaving the Entertainers Cafe for Louisville, then Dreamland and Royal Gardens, and a trumpeter relative who went back to New Orleans, probably Manuel Perez.
